subject: History
topic: Akbar's religious and administrative policy — mixed tiers
description: Sulh-i-kul, Din-i-Ilahi, Ibadat Khana, mansabdari, jizya abolition, court scholars

questions.stem: Akbar's policy of 'SULH-I-KUL' is best translated as:

options.option_text: Strict enforcement of Islamic religious orthodoxy
Universal peace and tolerance of all religions
Ban on all non-Persian languages used at court
Heavy taxes on Hindu landholders to fund armies

questions.explanation: SULH-I-KUL — Persian / Sufi-influenced phrase meaning 'absolute peace' or 'peace with all'. Akbar's foundational policy of religious tolerance: no one should be persecuted for faith; merit, not religion, decided imperial advancement. Practical expressions: abolition of pilgrim tax (1563), abolition of jizya on non-Muslims (1564), Rajput marriages (Mariam-uz-Zamani), Hindu generals (Raja Man Singh, Raja Todar Mal, Bhagwan Das). Counterpoint: Aurangzeb reversed many of these (re-imposed jizya 1679).

questions.stem: Akbar built the IBADAT KHANA at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575 specifically as:

options.option_text: A military headquarters for his Rajput cavalry units
A hall for inter-religious philosophical debates and dialogue
A public bathhouse with hot and cold water arrangements
A burial chamber for the early imperial Mughal ancestors

questions.explanation: Ibadat Khana ('House of Worship') — built 1575 inside Fatehpur Sikri. Initially for Sunni Muslim ulema; from 1578 opened to Shias, Sufis, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians (Parsis), Christian Jesuits (Aquaviva, Monserrate from Goa). Many notable theological debates held here. Akbar grew sceptical of orthodoxy, leading to his promulgation of DIN-I-ILAHI (1582), a syncretic ethical movement combining elements of multiple faiths — small following (~19 disciples), did not survive his death. Distractor 4 — Mughal tombs are separate (e.g., Humayun's tomb at Delhi, Akbar's own at Sikandra).

questions.stem: Akbar abolished the JIZYA tax — a tax historically levied on non-Muslims under Islamic rule — in:

options.option_text: 1556, the year of his accession after Humayun's death
1564, eight years into his independent reign
1582, with the founding of the Din-i-Ilahi religion
1605, just before his death in October that year

questions.explanation: Akbar abolished the JIZYA in 1564 — eight years into his reign (became king 1556 at age 13; Bairam Khan's regency ended 1560). Earlier in 1563 he had abolished pilgrim tax on Hindus. These were politically symbolic moves to win Hindu support — particularly Rajputs whose cooperation was vital for empire. Aurangzeb RE-IMPOSED jizya in 1679 (alienating Rajputs and contributing to imperial decline). Distractor 1 — Akbar was a child then, regents ran the empire. Distractor 3 — Din-i-Ilahi was 1582. Distractor 4 — too late.

questions.stem: The MANSABDARI system, introduced by Akbar, was primarily a:

options.option_text: System of land grants given outright to Hindu peasants
Ranking system for nobles linking civil and military service
Religious order encouraging mixed-faith Sufi devotion
Trade guild that controlled all the spice trade routes

questions.explanation: MANSABDARI — Persian 'mansab' (rank). Each noble (mansabdar) held a numerical rank, with two parts: ZAT (personal status / pay grade) and SAWAR (number of cavalry he must maintain for state service). Highest ranks (~5000+ zat) held by Mughal princes. Salaries paid in cash or as JAGIR (revenue assignment from a tract of land). System brought all civil + military officers into a single hierarchy, weakening hereditary tribal aristocracy. Continued and refined by successors. Distractor 1 = jagir / inam systems (different). Distractor 3 = sufi orders. Distractor 4 = guilds / European company analogy.

questions.stem: Akbar's revenue system, refined under his finance minister, settled land tax based on:

options.option_text: A simple flat-rate tax irrespective of crop or year
Detailed survey of land + 10-year average yield (Dahsala)
A share of village livestock paid to the local zamindar
A poll tax based on the number of male family members

questions.explanation: DAHSALA SYSTEM (also called the ZABTI system) — designed by RAJA TODAR MAL (Akbar's revenue minister, originally served Sher Shah Suri). 1580s. STEPS — measure land (bigha), classify by quality (polaj — annual; parauti — fallow then back; chachar — fallow 3-4 yrs; banjar — barren), record 10-year average yield + price for each crop, fix demand at one-third of average produce, payable in cash. Replaced earlier ad-hoc collections. Continued under later Mughals. Distractor 1 — too crude. Distractor 3 — separate, livestock-based. Distractor 4 = jizya structure, not land revenue.

questions.stem: The famous 'NINE GEMS' (Navaratnas) of Akbar's court included Abul Fazl, Birbal, Tansen, Todar Mal, Faizi, Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khana, Mulla Do Piaza, Hakim Humam, and one more. Who was the ninth gem?

options.option_text: Tulsidas, the Hindi poet of Ramcharitmanas fame
Raja Man Singh, Akbar's Rajput general and Amber ruler
Mirza Ghalib, the celebrated 19th-century Urdu poet
Bairam Khan, the regent during Akbar's early years

questions.explanation: Akbar's NAVARATNAS (Nine Gems): (1) ABUL FAZL — chronicler, author of Akbarnama + Ain-i-Akbari (assassinated 1602 by Bir Singh Bundela on Salim's orders); (2) FAIZI — poet, Abul Fazl's elder brother; (3) BIRBAL — court wit + counsellor (died 1586 in Yusufzai campaign); (4) TANSEN — court musician (originally Mian Tansen, from Gwalior, dhrupad master); (5) RAJA TODAR MAL — finance minister; (6) RAJA MAN SINGH — Rajput general (Amber); (7) ABDUR RAHIM KHAN-I-KHANA — poet, Bairam Khan's son; (8) FAQIR AZIAO-DIN; (9) MULLA DO PIAZA. Distractor 1 — Tulsidas was Akbar's contemporary but not in his court. Distractor 3 — much later (1797-1869). Distractor 4 — Bairam Khan was the regent (died 1561), not in the navaratnas.

questions.stem: Akbar's syncretic order DIN-I-ILAHI (1582) — sometimes called Tauhid-i-Ilahi — drew elements from many religions but was based ESSENTIALLY on:

options.option_text: Strict orthodox Sunni Islam alone, with no other influences
An ethical code emphasising piety, prudence, abstinence, sun-veneration
The Bhakti devotional movement of medieval north India alone
Christian doctrine introduced by Jesuit missionaries from Goa

questions.explanation: DIN-I-ILAHI ('Religion of God') / TAUHID-I-ILAHI ('Divine monotheism') — promulgated 1582. Drew from: Islam (especially Sufi monism), Hindu Vedanta + Bhakti, Zoroastrianism (sun + fire reverence), Jainism (vegetarianism, ahimsa), Christianity (love + reason). EMPHASES: piety, prudence, kindness, abstinence from meat / alcohol, abstinence from sensual indulgences, sun + fire veneration. NOT a mass religion — strictly elite court initiation; ~19 known disciples (incl. Birbal). Faded with Akbar's death (1605). Akbar himself viewed it as 'spiritual leadership of the empire' rather than displacement of existing faiths.
